abstract: We examine how negative environmental and social (E&S) incidents affect consumer behavior and firms’ responses. Using high-frequency store-visit data from SafeGraph linked to firm E&S incidents from RepRisk, we find that negative incidents lead to a modest decline in store visits on average, with substantially larger reductions among more environmentally and socially conscious consumers in Democratic-leaning areas. The effects are stronger for more severe and influential incidents, among younger and more educated consumers, for firms with higher pre-incident advertising intensity and E&S ratings, and in more competitive markets. Following these incidents, firms temporarily reduce discretionary disclosures and increase advertising expenditures over the longer run. Together, the results highlight consumer behavior as a way in which E&S incidents affect firm cash flows and suggest that firms adjust disclosure and advertising following these incidents.
title: From incidents to outcomes: consumer reactions and firm responses to negative environmental and social practices

abstract: The market for rare earth elements is relatively small in value, but shortages can lead to disproportionate output losses. This column introduces a network model to quantify the output losses from a large and permanent shortage of rare earth elements. At short horizons less than one year, GDP losses range from 0.6% in the UK to 1.5% in the US and 1.8% in Japan. Supply chain risk assessments need to incorporate production networks to understand the vulnerabilities from such disruptions. Policymakers should build strategic reserves and develop domestic capacity to help withstand the short-run losses from rare earth shortages.
authors: Christian Bogmans, Maximiliano Jerez Osses, Jorge Miranda-Pinto, Jean-Marc Natal

abstract: Temporary fuel-tax cuts are eventually restored, making both policy directions relevant for consumer incidence. Using ordinary and tax-exempt prices for the same gasoline and diesel in Korea, we compare two cuts and two restorations in 2018–2021. Over days 1–7 after each reform, full-sample, equal-event pass-through averages about 70% for cuts and 54–55% for restorations. Same-station comparisons and checks for sample composition, cost adjustment, and local shocks retain this point ordering. Pretrend and no-reform diagnostics nevertheless reveal differential price movements. Under stated restrictions, sensitivity bounds limit the size of a firm-favorable restoration-minus-cut gap, although the negative sign is less robust to departures from parallel trends. The results document incomplete initial consumer relief and lower estimated first-week pass-through when relief is withdrawn, with diagnostics quantifying the implications of differential price adjustment.
title: Does what goes up come back down? Pass-through of fuel-tax cuts and restorations in Korea

abstract: The EU's decision to phase out Russian natural gas imports raises concerns about the economic consequences of the ban, particularly its timing and uneven regional impacts. This paper examines how the wholesale gas price effects of eliminating Russian supplies depend on changing market conditions, including global LNG availability, infrastructure development and European gas demand. Using a European gas market model, we compare the impacts of an immediate phase-out under 2024 market conditions with those of a gradual phase-out under projected 2028 conditions, while distinguishing the effects of the ban from broader market developments. The results show that an immediate phase-out would lead to significant regional price increase, particularly in Central and South-Eastern Europe (4-5 €/MWh), where infrastructure constraints limit access to alternative supplies. By contrast, under projected 2028 market conditions, the ban would increase average EU wholesale gas prices by only 0.3 €/MWh and gas procurement costs by approximately 1%. Extending the phase-out to neighbouring non-EU countries would increase costs, particularly in the Western Balkans. Global market circumstances have by magnitude greater impact on absolute price levels than the Russian gas phaseout itself. The findings suggest that a coordinated phase-out of Russian gas can be achieved with limited additional wholesale market costs, provided that sufficient alternative supplies and infrastructure are available. They also highlight the importance of regional cooperation and continued supply diversification to mitigate uneven impacts across European gas markets.
title: Can Europe afford to phase out Russian gas? How timing, global supply conditions, and demand shape wholesale gas prices

abstract: This paper revisits fiscal policy in a currency union using a behavioral New Keynesian model with cognitive discounting à la Gabaix (2020). Cognitive discounting reshapes the government spending multiplier through three channels: a non-Ricardian effect, as households underweight future taxes; an expectation-dampening effect, which weakens forward inflation transmission; and a TOT effect, which slows terms-of-trade adjustment. At the ZLB, the welfare gain from discretionary fiscal coordination is positive but small in the two-country model. Stronger cognitive discounting generally reduces this gain by weakening inflation expectation transmission. Moreover, the gains are asymmetric: the directly shocked country benefits more, while its partner also benefits over the empirically relevant calibration range of cognitive discounting.
title: Fiscal policy in a behavioral New Keynesian model for the currency union
